findings:
Short version: under these rules the winning strategy is to eat a lot and fight little. Posturing behind a hazard does win, but only while the giants are careless around hazards, and the giants evolve their care back within about ten generations.

  1. Every run converged on the same core, whatever lineage it came from. Hunger goes to the maximum (2.0), greed rises to about 1.3–1.6, and split-strikes go to zero in all four runs. Wandering and gunning die out too. Grazers founded the winning lineage in three runs and hunters in the big arena, but the “hunter” champion never splits either: it is a grazer under a hunter's name. Two runs found two ways to stay safe: a wide threat radius with little fear (caution 1.65, fear 0.7), or a narrow radius with more fear and a bigger size margin (caution 0.34, fear 1.1, risk 1.2). Both work.
  2. Evolved genomes beat every hand-written preset. With all seven presets and the four champions in one arena, the champions win 87% of games (big arena: 89%). No preset wins more than 5% (the clan preset; the grazer wins 3%).
  3. Punishing the powerful never pays the punisher. The gunner drive (feed hazards to shoot them at giants) goes to about zero in every run. Gun hits keep happening by accident, and in most of them a third party collects the shards (kingmaking), as step 1 found.
  4. Posturing behind a hazard is an arms race. Under winner-takes-all fitness (time spent as the largest cell) the run goes through three phases:
    • gens 0–30: giants stop steering around hazards (thorn care 0.67 → 0.01). Carelessness pays: with no baiters around, careless giants hold the #1 spot 39% of the time against 33% for careful ones.
    • gens 30–60: small cells exploit them. Shelter rises 0.3 → 1.2, bait 0.25 → 1.4, and lures (a giant shatters chasing a cell posted by a hazard) go from 2 to 48 per game.
    • gens 60–72: thorn care comes back (0.19 → 1.17) in about ten generations, and lures fall to about zero.
    Controlled test with the crown champion's genome: baiters (bait 1.6, shelter 1.2) hold the #1 spot 42–47% of the time against careless giants but only 31% against careful ones, where they lose to plain foragers. So posturing pays only against a particular kind of opponent. Bait stays high in the population after the lures stop (1.3–1.4) even though it now costs a little. My reading is that it is a leftover from the arms race that selection hasn't removed yet. The same shorter cycle shows up in both “power” runs: thorn care collapses, lures peak at 8–10 per game around gen 30–40, then thorn care recovers.
  5. What you are rewarded for changes the society you get. Rewarding mass held over time produces peaceful foragers. Rewarding time at the top keeps hazards in play: about 100 post-ups per game at the end, against about 10 under the power fitness. In every run, though, the de-politicised twin of each champion (shelter, bait, shadow and gunner set to 0) does as well as or better than the champion itself, in a field of its own kind.
  6. Kin loyalty doesn't really evolve. Clans are heritable tags. The kin gene drifts low in three runs and reaches 0.4–0.6 in the big arena. Even there, the share of eating that is kin eating kin matches what random eating would give. The gene only stops an agent from chasing kin, and most eating happens by bumping into a cell, so kin get eaten anyway.

What surprised me: how fast the founder strategies disappear (within 10–15 generations), and that the most “political” run is the one where fitness is just being on top, not the one about holding power. The two runs with identical rules found different but equally good safety rules. And the jackal's betrayal (eating the giant it shadowed after the giant shatters) happens on its own, without the jackal preset.

Caveats: the population is small (42), games are noisy, and selection is strong, so lucky newcomers often top a single generation. Champions are chosen only from genomes tested in at least 36 games. Each regime ran once, except power, which ran twice. The moment detectors are heuristics. A post-up is any small cell sitting on a hazard within a giant's reach for 1.5 s, whether or not it meant to.
